passage:
"Dhruv, read this before I send it." Yogesh turned the laptop around on the dining table.
Dhruv read aloud. "'Third late login this month. Consider this your final warning. Excuses will not be entertained.' Who's it for?"
"Salma, on my team. She's always ten minutes late."
"Why?"
"No idea. Didn't ask."
"Would you talk to Ammi like this if she was late?"
Yogesh laughed, then didn't. "No. I'd ask if the bus broke down."
"So?"
Yogesh deleted the message. "I've become that supervisor, haven't I? The one we used to complain about."
"A bit."
"Okay. Tomorrow I ask her what's going on, first. And I'll ask my manager to look at how we handle lates, so it's not just my mood."
"And ask the team?"
"Anonymous form. 'What one thing do I do that makes work worse?'" Yogesh groaned. "That'll be fun."
"Fun for me," Dhruv grinned.

qa.q: What did Yogesh's draft message call it?
qa.a: A 'final warning' for a third late login this month.

qa.q: What does Yogesh's laugh that suddenly stops suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Yogesh suddenly sees the message is harsher than anything Yogesh would say at home, and feels uncomfortable at becoming the supervisor they used to complain about.

qa.q: Which choices did Yogesh make after deleting the message?
qa.a: To ask Salma what's going on first, to ask the manager to review how lates are handled, and to send the team an anonymous form.

qa.q: How might Salma have felt if she had received the first message?
qa.a: Salma would likely feel judged without being heard, since nobody had asked why she was late.

grounding: At home, a young supervisor asks whether they would treat family this way, then seeks a manager's review and honest team input.

passage: This is Jasleen, writing it down so I don't forget. Three months into supervising the packing floor at the warehouse, I caught myself timing Rajni's washroom breaks on the clipboard. Rajni is fifty and has two grandchildren. At a family wedding I'd give her my chair. Standing there with the clipboard, I asked myself: would I do this to my own Bua? The answer was so obviously no that I felt sick. That week I did three things. I wrote the break rules on the notice board, so nobody depended on my mood. I asked our HR head to sit in on one shift a month and tell me what they saw. And I left a box by the water cooler: 'What should I stop doing?' The first note said, 'Stop the clipboard.' I did.

qa.q: What was Jasleen timing on the clipboard?
qa.a: Rajni's washroom breaks.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen feel sick standing with the clipboard?
qa.a: Asking 'would I do this to my own Bua?' made the answer obviously no, and Jasleen was shaken by the gap between the work self and the real self.

qa.q: Which of Jasleen's three steps adds a check from outside, and why does that choice matter?
qa.a: Asking the HR head to sit in on one shift a month; someone outside the role can spot drift that Jasleen might miss.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel when the clipboard stops?
qa.a: Rajni would likely feel trusted and respected again, no longer watched like a suspect 🙂

grounding: A young supervisor asks whether they'd treat a worker this way outside work, then adds clear rules, oversight and honest feedback.

passage:
Ops head's note, Monday. Baljeet.
Lokesh has been shift supervisor on the bottling line for four months. I've watched him closely, since new supervisors here often turn sharp by month three. Last week I saw him start to shout at Kiran over a jammed conveyor, then stop mid-sentence. Afterwards he came to my cabin. 'Sir, I was about to talk to her the way I'd never talk to anyone outside this gate. Can you sit in on my Friday huddles for a while?' He also asked to put the line targets and his own performance notes on the board, so the team sees what he is judged on. At the huddle he asked, 'What am I doing that makes your day harder?' Two people answered.
What I did next: I agreed to join Fridays and suggested the other supervisors try the same practice.

qa.q: What was Lokesh about to shout at Kiran over?
qa.a: A jammed conveyor.

qa.q: What does Lokesh stopping mid-sentence suggest he was thinking?
qa.a: It suggests Lokesh felt alarmed on noticing he was about to treat Kiran in a way he never would outside the gate, and caught the role taking over.

qa.q: Which of Lokesh's requests made his work more open to checks?
qa.a: Asking Baljeet to sit in on Friday huddles, and putting the line targets and his own performance notes on the board for the team to see.

qa.q: How might Kiran see a supervisor who stops mid-shout?
qa.a: Kiran might feel relieved and more willing to speak honestly at huddles, seeing a supervisor who checks himself.

grounding: An ops head records a young supervisor catching himself, inviting oversight, sharing targets openly and asking the team for input.

passage:
Tuesday, after shift

Three months as housekeeping supervisor at the hotel. Today I caught myself. Zubin had missed a corner under a bed in 412, and I was standing over him with the checklist, saying, "How many times do I have to tell you people?" He's twenty-two, sends half his pay home, and always holds the lift for guests.

I stopped mid-sentence and asked myself: would I talk to Zubin like this at the bus stop? No. Never.

So what's happening to me in that uniform?

Three things I did today:
1. Wrote the room-check rules on the staff board, so it's the rule, not my mood.
2. Asked the front-office manager to walk my floors with me once a week and tell me honestly what she sees.
3. At the evening huddle I said, "Tell me one thing I do that makes your work harder." Silence. Then Zubin said, "Standing over us, ma'am." Fair.

- Ritu

qa.q: Which room had Zubin missed a corner in?
qa.a: He missed a corner under a bed in room 412.

qa.q: What made Ritu stop mid-sentence?
qa.a: She suddenly asked herself whether she would speak to Zubin like that at the bus stop and knew she would never, which showed her the role was changing her.

qa.q: Which of Ritu's three steps protects most against the role taking over, and why?
qa.a: Writing the rules on the board and asking the front-office manager to walk her floors make things transparent and checked, so her mood no longer decides.

qa.q: How might Zubin have felt saying 'Standing over us' at the huddle?
qa.a: He was probably nervous but relieved to be asked, and it may have made him trust his supervisor more.

grounding: A young supervisor asks whether she would treat a worker this way outside work, then adds clear rules, outside oversight and a request for honest input.

passage: On the road-work site near her village, Noor, twenty-five, had been made supervisor of forty labourers. By the second week she'd started shouting, cutting wages for small delays, and refusing water breaks until noon. One afternoon Raghav, an older labourer, fainted from the heat. Noor ran over, got him into the shade and gave him water, and called the health worker, who came at once. Sitting by him, she felt sick with shame. Would I treat my own uncle like this? she thought. That evening she called the workers together. "I've been too harsh. Tell me honestly what's wrong." They were silent, then one by one they spoke: the water, the wage cuts, the shouting. Noor wrote it down. She asked the block officer to visit weekly and posted the break times on a board for everyone to see.

qa.q: How many labourers did Noor supervise?
qa.a: Noor had been made supervisor of forty labourers.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling as she sat by Raghav?
qa.a: Noor felt sick with shame, realising she'd treated the workers in a way she never would outside work.

qa.q: Which of Noor's steps protect against role drift, and why?
qa.a: Asking workers for honest input, inviting the block officer to visit, and posting break times make her power visible and checked.

qa.q: How might the workers have felt when Noor asked for honest feedback?
qa.a: The workers were hesitant at first, then relieved to be heard as people rather than just labour.

grounding: A young supervisor notices harsh role drift, asks whether she'd treat someone this way outside work, seeks oversight and invites honest input.

passage: Nkechi, twenty-six, had been a team supervisor at the Lagos call centre for three months. One Friday she caught herself standing over a new agent, arms crossed, timing his toilet break. She stopped. Would I do this to my brother? she thought. Then she noticed her own face in the glass: stern, cold, someone she didn't recognise. That afternoon she asked Ingrid, the operations manager, to sit in on her team meetings once a week. "Tell me if I'm being unfair." She also set up an anonymous box where agents could leave feedback. The first note said, "You don't say good morning anymore." Nkechi laughed, a bit painfully. On Monday she said good morning to every agent, by name, and wrote the break rules on the board so they applied to everyone, including her.

qa.q: What did the first anonymous note say?
qa.a: The first note said, "You don't say good morning anymore."

qa.q: What was Nkechi feeling when she saw her own face in the glass?
qa.a: Nkechi felt uneasy and shocked, not recognising the stern, cold person the role had made her.

qa.q: Which of Nkechi's actions protect against role drift?
qa.a: Inviting Ingrid to observe, setting up an anonymous feedback box, and applying clear break rules to everyone including herself.

qa.q: How might the new agent have felt when Nkechi timed his break?
qa.a: The new agent likely felt watched and humiliated, treated as a suspect rather than a colleague.

grounding: A young supervisor notices role drift, asks whether she'd treat someone this way outside work, seeks oversight and invites honest feedback.

passage: Deepika, twenty-four, had become assistant warden of the girls' hostel in Coimbatore. Within a month, she noticed she was enjoying catching girls after curfew. She'd started doing surprise checks at two a.m., reading out names at dinner. One night, Rukmini, a second-year, came in ten minutes late, crying; her bus had broken down. Deepika had already opened the register when she saw her face. She put the pen down. If this were my little sister, would I write her up? No. She sat with Rukmini, got her some water and let her call her mother. The next day Deepika asked the senior warden to review every late entry with her each week, and held a meeting where students could speak honestly about the rules. Rukmini was the first to raise her hand.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she saw Rukmini's face?
qa.a: Deepika felt a pang of concern and doubt, realising she was enjoying the role's power too much.

qa.q: What did Deepika do to step out of the role?

qa.q: How might Rukmini have felt at the meeting?

passage:
Subject: Something I noticed about myself
Dear Leela,
You mentored me before I became floor supervisor at the garment unit, so I wanted to tell you this.
Last Monday I shouted at a tailor for being five minutes late. I made her sit apart. Walking home, I asked myself: would I treat an aunty in my building this way? No.
So I've done three things. I've asked the HR officer to sit in on any warnings I give. I've put a box by the door for anonymous comments about me. And I've started asking the tailors each Friday, "What would make this week easier?"
The tailor I shouted at said the bus had broken down. I said sorry.
Kavitha

qa.a: Kavitha put a box by the door for anonymous comments.

qa.a: Asking HR to sit in on warnings adds oversight, so no warning can be given harshly without someone watching.

passage:
Eshaan, you asked how I handle being a shift head at twenty-five. I'm Indu, and honestly, I nearly lost it in the first month.
The job gives you a lot of power over the nurses. I found myself snapping, "Just do it," not listening to reasons. One night a nurse said a patient needed a second opinion, and I told her to stop wasting time.
She was right. That shook me.
Now I ask myself before each order: would I say this to her if we met at a wedding? I've asked the nursing director to review my rotas every month. And every Sunday I sit with the nurses for ten minutes and ask, "What am I getting wrong?"
It's uncomfortable. It's also working.

qa.q: How often does the nursing director review Indu's rotas?
qa.a: The director reviews them every month.

qa.q: What did Indu feel when the nurse turned out to be right?
qa.a: Indu felt shaken and embarrassed, seeing how the role had made listening stop.

qa.q: What could another new supervisor learn from Indu?
qa.a: They could check each order against how they'd speak outside work, ask for oversight, and invite honest feedback from the team.

qa.q: How might the nurses feel in the Sunday meetings?
qa.a: They may feel heard and more respected, able to say what's wrong without fear.

grounding: Shows a young supervisor checking each order against how they would speak outside work, seeking oversight and asking the team for honest input.

passage:
I've worked under Sharmila at the call centre for a year. I'm Kunal, one of her team.
In her first months as supervisor she was harsh. She timed toilet breaks to the second. She read out our call scores in front of everyone.
Then, one Monday, she called a meeting. "I've been acting like someone I don't like," she said. "Tell me, honestly, what's been hard."

She also asked her own manager to sit in on her reviews. And she pinned a sheet by the door: "We're people first."
I noticed I started speaking up in meetings again.

passage: Lavanya, you've just become warden and I can see you stiffening already, so let me tell you about my first year. I was twenty-five, warden of a girls' hostel in Coimbatore. Within months I was checking bags at the gate, reading out late names at dinner, treating every girl like a suspect. One night I shouted at a student who had come back late from visiting her grandmother in hospital. She cried, and I felt powerful. Then on the bus home I thought: Shalini, would you speak to your own niece like this? No. So I did three things. I asked the principal to sit in on one hostel meeting a month. I put a box in the mess for anonymous complaints about me. And every Friday I ate dinner with the girls, not at the warden's table. The complaints were painful to read. But I stayed a person, not a warden.

qa.a: They brought oversight and honest input, keeping the role's power in check and reminding her the students were people.

qa.q: How might the student returning from the hospital visit have felt when shouted at?
qa.a: She likely felt hurt and unfairly treated, already worried about her grandmother.

passage: The monsoon was two weeks away, and the site in Pune was behind schedule. Eshaan, supervising his first crew, had started to change. He shouted at the workers for tea breaks and threatened to cut wages for slow bricklaying. On Thursday he found himself yelling at Madhav Kaka, the oldest mason, for sitting down in the heat. Madhav Kaka stood up slowly, without a word. That silence stopped Eshaan. He thought: I'd never talk to my own grandfather like this. That evening he called the project manager and asked her to visit the site weekly and see how he ran it. The next morning he gathered the crew. 'I've been harsh. Tell me what's making the work slow.' Madhav Kaka spoke first: the cement arrived late every day, and there was no shade for breaks. Eshaan fixed both. They finished the roof four days before the rain.

qa.a: The cement arrived late every day, and there was no shade for breaks.

qa.q: Which steps helped Eshaan step out of the harsh role?
qa.a: Inviting the project manager to check weekly, admitting he'd been harsh, and asking the crew for honest input.

qa.q: How might Madhav Kaka have felt being asked for his view?
qa.a: Madhav Kaka probably felt respected and relieved, finally heard after being shouted at.

passage: Urmila had been team leader at the Noida call centre for four months when she caught herself mid-sentence. Hrithik, nineteen, had come back from a break three minutes late, and she was halfway through "Do you think this is your home?" in front of the whole row. She stopped. Would she talk to her cousin like this? To anyone at a family lunch? That evening she did three things. She asked her own manager to sit in on her team huddles for a month and tell her honestly what she saw. She wrote the break rules on the whiteboard, the same for everyone, including her. And she handed out slips of paper: "One thing I do that makes your day harder. No names." Nine of eleven came back. Four said "shouting". The next morning she apologised to Hrithik, in front of the same row.

qa.q: How many of the eleven slips came back?
qa.a: Nine of eleven.

qa.q: Why did Urmila stop mid-sentence?
qa.a: She felt a jolt of shame, realising she would never speak to a cousin or anyone at a family lunch that way.

qa.q: Which of Urmila's steps guard best against role drift?
qa.a: Asking her manager to watch her huddles, posting the same break rules for all and collecting anonymous feedback add oversight, clear limits and honest input.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel when Urmila apologises in front of the same row?
qa.a: Hrithik would likely feel respected and relieved, since the apology is as public as the scolding was.
